quizTitle: Project Management - Module 6: Requirements Traceability Matrix

questions.text: What is the core purpose of a Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM)?
options: To schedule project activities and their durations
To connect business goals to deliverables, design, and QA testing
To list every stakeholder and their level of influence
To record the project's budget baseline and cost variances
questions.explanation: The RTM's core purpose is to connect business goals to deliverables, design, and QA testing, so every requirement can be followed from why it exists to how it was verified. Scheduling, stakeholder registers and budget baselines are separate artifacts.

questions.text: The RTM is often explained with a laptop order: you order 32GB RAM, a 1TB SSD and a backlit keyboard, and when the box arrives you check the packing slip directly against the order invoice. What does checking the packing slip against the invoice stand for?
questions.explanation: Ordering the specs is the user specification; checking the slip against the invoice is delivery verification. The RTM is the master checklist that makes sure every requested feature is built and verified.

questions.text: Which sequence correctly orders the PMBOK traceability lineage, from origin to QA?
options: Business Goal → Requirement → WBS Package → System Design → Test Case ID
Requirement → Business Goal → System Design → WBS Package → Test Case ID
Business Goal → WBS Package → Requirement → Test Case ID → System Design
Test Case ID → System Design → WBS Package → Requirement → Business Goal
questions.explanation: The lineage runs Business Goal (Origin) → Requirement (Anchor) → WBS Package (Scope) → System Design (Design) → Test Case ID (QA). The last option is the same chain read backwards, not the origin-to-QA order.

questions.text: Match each stage of the PMBOK traceability lineage to the item that sits there.
questions.explanation: The requirement is the anchor: backward it links to the business goal (origin); forward it links to the WBS package (scope), the system design, and the test case (QA).

questions.text: In an RTM, what does backward traceability link a requirement to?
options: The test case that verifies it
The WBS work package that builds it
The business goal in the Project Charter or business case
The system module or API that implements it
questions.explanation: Backward traceability goes to goals: it links the requirement back to the business goal (Project Charter / strategic need) that justifies it. The WBS package, design and test case are all forward links, toward verification.

questions.text: In an RTM, what does forward traceability link a requirement to?
options: The business goal that justifies it
The Project Charter that authorized the project
Its WBS package, system design, and test case, through to verification
questions.explanation: Forward traceability goes to verification: requirement → WBS package → system design → test case ID. It answers "was it built, and how do we know it works?"

questions.text: A PM checks that every requirement in the RTM can be traced back to an objective in the Project Charter. This check is an example of forward traceability.
questions.explanation: False. Linking a requirement back to a Charter objective is backward traceability (to goals). Forward traceability links it on to the WBS package, design, and test case (to verification).

questions.text: Six months into a project, the client asks: "Why did we spend $50k on features nobody asked for?" Which problem would a properly maintained RTM have prevented?
questions.explanation: The RTM is the PM's defense against scope creep: every feature must trace back to an approved requirement, which blocks unauthorized features added without strategic approval.

questions.text: Near the end of a project, the client asks: "Where is the feature I asked for six months ago?" Which problem would a properly maintained RTM have prevented?
questions.explanation: The RTM prevents omissions by guaranteeing 100% scope coverage: every requirement is tracked through to a deliverable and a test, so none is forgotten.

questions.text: Match each standard RTM field to the document or source it comes from.
questions.explanation: Each RTM column is filled from a specific source: IDs from the requirements documentation, statements from the BA and stakeholders, objectives from the Charter or business case, WBS codes from the completed WBS baseline, design modules from the System Design Document, and test case IDs from the QA Plan.

questions.text: Which RTM field records the strategic rationale that justifies why a requirement exists at all?
questions.explanation: The Business Objective field holds the strategic rationale, taken from the Project Charter or business case. It is the backward link of each row.

questions.text: In an RTM, the ___ field holds the Work Package ID responsible for creating the deliverable. (Two words.)
questions.explanation: The WBS Code field cross-references the exact work package from the completed WBS baseline that will produce the requirement's deliverable.

questions.text: In an RTM, which field names the architecture subsystem, API, database, or UI element that implements a requirement?
questions.explanation: The Design Module field records the architecture piece (subsystem, API, database or UI element), taken from the System Design Document.

questions.text: Put the 6 steps for constructing an RTM in order.
questions.explanation: The order follows the lineage: list requirements with unique IDs, link them back to the business need, map the WBS work package, define the technical spec, assign the test case, then track status through formal sign-off.

questions.text: When constructing an RTM, which step establishes the backward link from each requirement to the Project Charter's objectives?
questions.explanation: Step 2, Link Business Need, establishes the backward link to the Project Charter objectives.

questions.text: When constructing an RTM, in which step do you specify the QA scripts and measurable acceptance criteria for each requirement?
questions.explanation: Step 5, Assign Test Cases, specifies the QA scripts and measurable acceptance criteria. Define Technical Specs (Step 4) identifies modules, APIs or database tables instead.

questions.text: What does the final RTM construction step, Track & Baseline, involve?
options: Listing functional and non-functional requirements with unique IDs
Maintaining each requirement's execution status through formal sign-off
Choosing which requirements to cut when the budget runs short
questions.explanation: Track & Baseline maintains the execution status of each requirement (e.g., Not Started, In Dev, Passed QA) through formal sign-off.

questions.text: During an RTM review, you find a requirement that has no WBS Code. What is this flaw called?
questions.explanation: A requirement with no WBS Code is an orphaned requirement: no work package is responsible for it, so the promised feature is forgotten in the budget and schedule.

questions.text: A WBS work package exists in the project plan, but no requirement in the RTM traces to it. What is this flaw called, and what is its impact?
options: Orphaned requirement: a promised feature is left out of the budget
Quality blindspot: the deliverable has no verification method
Gold plating: money is spent on work nobody requested
Scope omission: the client's request is forgotten
questions.explanation: A WBS package with no requirement is gold plating: wasteful spending on unrequested work. (An orphaned requirement is the reverse: a requirement with no WBS code.)

questions.text: A requirement in the RTM has a Req ID, a business objective, a WBS code, and a design module, but its Test Case ID is blank. What is the impact of this flaw?
options: The feature is forgotten in the budget and schedule
The deliverable gets built without any method to verify it
Money is spent on unrequested work
The requirement can't be traced back to a business goal
questions.explanation: A missing Test Case ID is a quality blindspot: the deliverable is built without a verification method, so nobody can prove the requirement was met.

questions.text: An RTM excerpt is shown above (a dash means the cell is empty, and WBS 1.6.2 is a work package in the plan). Match each row to the scope flaw it shows.
questions.context:
Req IDRequirementWBS CodeTest Case ID
REQ-01Students can download their grade report as a PDF—TC-01
REQ-02Instructors can post announcements to a courseWBS 1.3.1—
—(no requirement traces here)WBS 1.6.2 Animated 3D campus tour—
questions.explanation: No WBS code = orphaned requirement (forgotten in budget and schedule). No test case = quality blindspot (built without verification). A WBS package with no requirement = gold plating (spending on unrequested work).

questions.text: What is the core distinction between functional (FR) and non-functional (NFR) requirements?
options: FRs are tested by QA; NFRs are never tested
FRs come from the client; NFRs come from the development team
FRs are mandatory; NFRs are optional nice-to-haves
FRs describe WHAT the system does; NFRs describe HOW WELL it performs
questions.explanation: FR = WHAT it does (features, user actions, business logic). NFR = HOW WELL it performs (operational thresholds, security, constraints). NFRs are not optional and they are tested, often with automated load or security tests.

questions.text: Classify each requirement as functional (FR) or non-functional (NFR).

pairs.term: Students can select and register for available course subjects.
The system supports 5,000 concurrent logins with a 2.0s load time.
Transcript records are encrypted under Data Privacy regulations.
The app issues a 6-digit SMS OTP for transfers over $500.
The OTP arrives within 5 seconds at 99.9% reliability.
Users can log in with fingerprint or FaceID.

questions.explanation: Registering for subjects, sending an OTP, and biometric login are things the system does (FR). Concurrent-login load time (performance), encryption under privacy law (security and compliance), and OTP delivery time and reliability are about how well it performs (NFR).

questions.text: Using a car as an analogy, which statement is the non-functional requirement?
options: Pressing the pedal makes the car accelerate forward
Turning the wheel steers the car
The car goes from 0 to 100 km/h in 4.5 seconds at 18 km/L efficiency
Pressing the brake stops the car
questions.explanation: The acceleration time and fuel efficiency say how well the car performs, so that's the NFR. The pedal, wheel and brake describe what the car does (FRs).

questions.text: Match each non-functional requirement to its pillar (the 4 pillars of NFRs, per ISO/IEC 25010 and PMBOK).

pairs.term: Balance queries return in under 1.0s with 10,000 concurrent users.
Card data is encrypted and handled per PCI-DSS.
The system targets 99.99% availability, with automatic failover.
Pages meet WCAG 2.1 AA and work across major browsers.

questions.explanation: Performance & Scale = response times, throughput, concurrent users. Security & Compliance = encryption, PCI-DSS, GDPR, HIPAA. Reliability & Uptime = availability targets, disaster recovery, failover. Usability & Access = mobile responsiveness, cross-browser support, WCAG 2.1 AA.

questions.text: Which standard defines the 4 pillars of non-functional requirements (Performance & Scale, Security & Compliance, Reliability & Uptime, Usability & Access), alongside PMBOK?
questions.explanation: The 4 pillars are drawn from ISO/IEC 25010 (the software product quality model) and PMBOK. PCI-DSS is a payment-security standard that appears as an example under the Security & Compliance pillar.

questions.text: A requirement reads: "Query responds in 1.0s under 10,000 requests." Which WBS work and QA test best fit it?
options: A frontend UI feature work package, verified by a pass/fail functional prompt
DB read replicas and a Redis caching layer, verified by an automated JMeter load test
A user training package, verified by a stakeholder survey
A new login screen, verified by manual exploratory testing
questions.explanation: This is a performance NFR. It maps to infrastructure work (DB read replicas, Redis caching) and is verified by automated load testing (a JMeter script), not a simple pass/fail check.

questions.text: A requirement reads: "Allow users to log in with biometrics." Which WBS work and QA test best fit it?
options: A penetration testing contract, verified by an external audit
DB read replicas and a caching layer, verified by load testing
A disaster-recovery site, verified by a failover drill
A frontend UI feature work package, verified by a standard pass/fail functional test
questions.explanation: Biometric login is a functional requirement: it maps to a frontend UI feature work package and is verified with a standard pass/fail functional test (does the login prompt work or not).

questions.text: Complete the principle: "Functional features build the product; Non-Functional requirements ___ ." (Three words.)
questions.explanation: "Functional features build the product; Non-Functional requirements keep it alive." A system can be feature-complete and still crash on launch day if its NFRs were ignored.

questions.text: A team building a university enrollment portal lists every functional requirement, but completely forgets this one: "The system supports 5,000 concurrent logins with a 2.0s load time." What is the most likely outcome on the first day of enrollment?
options: The portal has every feature but slows down or crashes under the enrollment rush
Students can't find the registration page
Nothing changes, since all the features were built
questions.explanation: The forgotten requirement is a performance NFR. Every feature can work in testing, yet the portal buckles when thousands of students log in at once: feature-complete, but down on launch day.

questions.text: A developer adds an unrequested "Dark Mode" feature that took only 2 hours to code. As PM, what should you do with it?
options: Add it directly, since it was cheap and users may like it
Update the RTM afterwards so the feature is documented
Route it through formal change control
questions.explanation: Route it through formal change control, which evaluates its business value, budget, and test impacts. Adding it directly bypasses change management and risks unverified scope creep; editing the RTM afterwards retroactively justifies unapproved work.

questions.text: A developer added an unrequested 2-hour "Dark Mode" feature, and someone suggests simply adding a row to the RTM after the fact. What is wrong with this?
options: The RTM can't hold UI requirements
It retroactively justifies work that was never approved
It makes the feature impossible to test
Nothing; this is the standard process
questions.explanation: A post-hoc RTM edit retroactively justifies unapproved work. The RTM should record approved scope, so new features go through change control first.

questions.text: An unrequested feature that takes only a couple of hours to build is too small to count as scope creep, so it can be added without change control.
questions.explanation: False. Size doesn't decide scope. An unrequested feature has no requirement behind it (gold plating), and adding it directly bypasses change management and risks unverified scope creep.

questions.text: Which requirement in this RTM is non-functional?
questions.context:
Req IDRequirement DescriptionBusiness Objective
REQ-AUTH-01Biometric login (Fingerprint / FaceID)Reduce support calls by 25%
REQ-PAY-042FA OTP for transactions over $500Comply with PCI-DSS standards
REQ-PERF-01Balance queries respond in under 1.0sEnsure peak load satisfaction
questions.explanation: REQ-PERF-01 sets a response-time threshold (how well), so it's a performance NFR. Biometric login and sending a 2FA OTP are things the system does (FRs), even though the OTP one is motivated by a compliance objective.

questions.text: An RTM row is complete once it has a Req ID, a requirement statement, and a WBS code.
questions.explanation: False. A complete row needs both linkages: the backward link (a business objective) and the full forward link (WBS code, design module, and a test case ID with acceptance criteria). Without a test case, it's a quality blindspot.

questions.text: When building a group RTM in the hands-on activity, which items are mandatory checks for each row? (Select all that apply.)
options: The exact WBS work package code
A test case ID and acceptance criteria
questions.explanation: The three mandatory checks are a clear business goal link (backward), the exact WBS work package code, and a test case ID with acceptance criteria (forward). Rates and schedule dates aren't RTM fields.

questions.text: In the hands-on activity to build a group RTM, how many requirements does each group select to populate the matrix?
questions.explanation: Each group opens its Requirements Doc and completed WBS Dictionary and selects 3 functional + 1 non-functional requirement to populate the template.
